blocks.text: A variable is simply a named box that holds a value. You put something in the box, give the box a name, and then use that name whenever you need the value again.

blocks.alt: Variables and data types: int, string, bool

blocks.text: Variables are how a program remembers things while it runs: a score, a username, the price of an item, or whether a setting is on or off. Without variables, a program could not keep track of anything.

Think of a variable as a labelled jar on a shelf. The label is the name you choose, and whatever you store inside is the value. You can look inside any time by its name, or swap the contents for something new.
You create a variable by giving it a name and a value. The value goes into the box, and the name is how you find it later.

codes.python:
age = 20            # a whole number
price = 19.99       # a number with decimals
name = "Riya"       # text
is_active = True    # true or false

blocks.text: Notice that in Python you do not say what kind of value it is, while in Java and C++ you state the type up front. We will explain why shortly.
How Variables Live in Memory

It helps to picture what is really happening. Your computer has memory, like a huge wall of numbered lockers. When you create a variable, the computer reserves a locker, puts your value inside, and lets you use the name instead of the locker number.
When you read the variable, the computer opens that locker and hands you a copy of the value. When you assign a new value, it replaces what is inside.
You never have to think about locker numbers. The variable name is a friendly label the computer maps to the right spot in memory for you.
The whole point of a variable is that it can vary. You can give it a new value any time, and you can even build the new value out of the old one.

codes.python:
score = 10
print(score)        # 10

score = 25          # replace the value completely
print(score)        # 25

score = score + 5   # use the old value to make a new one
print(score)        # 30

blocks.text: That third line surprises beginners. Read it right to left: first the computer works out score plus 5, which is 30, and then it stores 30 back into score. The old value is used, then replaced.
Reading a variable does not change it. Only an assignment with the equals sign changes what is stored inside.
Common Data Types
A data type tells the computer what kind of value a variable holds. This matters because you can do different things with different types. You can add numbers, but joining text works differently.
These five types cover almost everything you will touch in your first months.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Type","Holds","Example"],"rows":[["Integer","Whole numbers","42, 7, 0"],["Float or Double","Numbers with decimals","3.14, 0.5"],["Character","A single character","'A', '9'"],["Boolean","Either true or false","true, false"],["String","Text of any length","\"hello\""]]}

blocks.text: A closer look at each

items: Integer: counting numbers with no decimal point, used for ages, counts, indexes.
Float: numbers with a decimal point, used for prices, averages, measurements.
Character: exactly one letter, digit, or symbol.
Boolean: a yes or no value, the foundation of all decisions.
String: a sequence of characters, used for names, messages, and any text.

blocks.text: Integers are whole numbers, the workhorse of most programs. They are used for counting, indexing, and any value without a fraction.

In some languages like Java and C++, an integer has a maximum size. If a value grows past that limit, it can overflow and wrap around to a wrong, sometimes negative, number. This is a classic source of tricky bugs.
Python is friendly here: its integers grow as large as your memory allows, so overflow is not a concern. In Java and C++, watch out when numbers get very large.
Why Decimals Can Be Imprecise
Floating point numbers, meaning decimals, hold a surprise. Because of how computers store them, some values cannot be represented exactly.
This is not a bug in your code. It is how nearly all computers handle decimals. The tiny error is usually harmless, but it means you should avoid comparing two decimals for exact equality.
For money, many programmers avoid decimals entirely and store amounts as whole numbers of paise or cents, sidestepping the precision problem completely.
Strings, meaning text, are so common that they deserve their own moment. A string is just a sequence of characters wrapped in quotation marks.

codes.python:
first = "Riya"
last = "Sharma"
full = first + " " + last     # joining strings is called concatenation
print(full)                    # Riya Sharma
print(len(full))               # 11, the number of characters

blocks.text: You can join strings together, measure their length, and pull out individual characters. You cannot do math on them, because they are text, not numbers, even if they look like a number.
The string "123" and the number 123 look the same to you, but not to the computer. One is text, the other is a value you can do math with. Keep them straight and you avoid a whole class of bugs.
Booleans in More Depth
A boolean holds only two possible values: true or false. They look tiny, but they are the foundation of every decision a program makes.

codes.python:
is_raining = True
has_umbrella = False

print(is_raining and has_umbrella)   # False
print(is_raining or has_umbrella)    # True
print(not is_raining)                # False

blocks.text: Comparisons also produce booleans. Asking whether 5 is greater than 3 gives back true. Every if statement you ever write is really just checking a boolean.
Sometimes a value is the wrong type for what you want to do. Converting one type into another is called casting, and it is a daily task, especially with input.

codes.python:
age_text = "20"
age = int(age_text)     # text into a number
print(age + 5)          # 25

pi = 3.99
print(int(pi))          # 3, the decimals are simply dropped
print(str(age))         # a number back into text: "20"

blocks.text: An important surprise
Converting a decimal into an integer does not round it. It simply cuts off the decimal part. So 3.99 becomes 3, not 4. Remember this or your calculations may be off by one.
Most conversion bugs come from either forgetting to convert at all, or expecting rounding when the language actually just chops off the decimals.
Two Styles of Typing
Languages handle types in one of two ways, and knowing which one you use saves a lot of confusion.
Dynamically typed (like Python)

You do not state the type. The language works it out from the value, and a variable can even hold a different type later. This is flexible and quick to write, but a type mistake might not show up until the program runs.

codes.python:
x = 5        # x is a number now
x = "hello"  # perfectly allowed, x is text now

blocks.text: Statically typed (like Java and C++)
You declare the type up front and the variable keeps it for life. This feels stricter, but it catches a whole class of mistakes before the program even runs, which is valuable in large projects.

codes.java:
int x = 5;
x = "hello";   // error, caught before the program runs

blocks.text: Neither style is better. They are just different points on the line between flexibility and safety. Python favours flexibility, Java and C++ favour safety.
A common little task is swapping the values of two variables, so that each ends up holding what the other had. It shows up constantly in sorting and other algorithms.

codes.python:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a       # Python swaps in one clean line
print(a, b)       # 2 1

blocks.text: In Python you can swap in a single line. In most other languages you need a third temporary variable to avoid losing a value. Both achieve the same result.
Naming Variables Well
A good name makes code read almost like plain English. This is not a style nicety, it genuinely makes your code easier to understand and fix, including for your future self.

items: Prefer clear names: totalPrice beats tp
Start with a letter and stick to letters, digits, and underscores
Be consistent: pick one style such as userName or user_name and keep it everywhere
Save single letters like i and j for short loop counters only
Avoid names that lie, like calling something count when it holds a price

blocks.text: Good names vs weak names

codes.python:
# weak: what do these even mean?
x = 19.99
y = 3

# clear: the names explain themselves
item_price = 19.99
quantity = 3
total = item_price * quantity

blocks.text: You write a variable name once but read it many times. Spend the extra second to choose a name that explains itself, and your code becomes far easier to work with.

Sometimes a value should never change while the program runs, like the number of days in a week or a tax rate. These are called constants. Many languages let you mark a value as constant so it cannot be changed by accident.
Even when a language does not enforce it, programmers often use all capital letters to signal "do not change this", such as MAX_SIZE or PI. It is a helpful hint to anyone reading the code.

content.title: 8. Numbers vs Text: The Big Confusion

blocks.text: The most common early confusion is treating a number and its text form as the same thing. They are not, and the computer keeps them strictly apart.

codes.python:
a = "5"      # this is text
b = 5        # this is a number

print(a + a)   # 55, text is joined
print(b + b)   # 10, numbers are added

blocks.text: Both look like a five to you, but the first is text and the second is a value you can do math with. Adding text joins it, while adding numbers sums them.
Whenever math gives a strange result, ask yourself: is this value actually a number, or is it text that only looks like one?
You will very often update a variable using its own current value, like adding to a running total. There is a clean shortcut for this called augmented assignment.

codes.python:
total = 0
total += 10     # same as total = total + 10
total -= 3      # same as total = total - 3
total *= 2      # same as total = total * 2
print(total)    # 14

blocks.text: So total += 10 is just a shorter way of writing total = total + 10. It reads cleanly and you will see it constantly, especially inside loops.
Where you create a variable decides where it can be used. This idea is called scope. A variable made inside a block or a function usually lives only there.

You do not need the deep details yet. Just know that a variable is not always visible everywhere in your program, and that this is a good thing, because it keeps different parts from interfering with each other.
If your program complains that a variable is not defined, it may exist somewhere, just not in the place you are trying to use it. That is scope at work.
With a few types available, beginners often wonder which one to use. Here is a simple guide.

items: Counting something with no fraction? Use an integer.
Money, averages, or measurements? Use a float, or store money as whole paise.
A yes or no answer? Use a boolean.
Names, messages, or anything with letters? Use a string.

blocks.text: When in doubt, ask what you will do with the value. If you will do math, it should be a number. If it is words, it is a string.
Picking the right type early prevents a surprising number of bugs later. The type is a promise about what the value means.

items: Using a variable before giving it a value
Mixing up text and numbers, then being surprised math does not work
Expecting a decimal to round when converting to an integer
Comparing two decimals for exact equality despite tiny precision errors
Reusing one vague variable for several unrelated things
Tiny, unclear names that make the code impossible to follow later

blocks.text: When a variable holds something unexpected, print it right before the line that breaks. Seeing the real value is the fastest way to understand what went wrong.
Do I have to declare the type in Python?
No. Python figures out the type from the value. Java and C++ require you to state it.
Why did my big number turn negative in Java?
That is integer overflow. The value grew past the maximum an integer can hold and wrapped around. Use a larger number type or Python, where integers grow freely.
Why is 0.1 plus 0.2 not exactly 0.3?
Because computers cannot store some decimals exactly. It is normal. Avoid comparing decimals for exact equality.
What is the difference between a character and a string?
A character is exactly one symbol. A string is a sequence of any number of characters, including zero.

items: Variable: a named box that holds a value.
Data type: the kind of value a variable holds.
Assignment: giving a variable a value with the equals sign.
Casting: converting a value from one type to another.
Overflow: a number growing past the maximum its type can hold.
Constant: a value that should not change while the program runs.
Store your name, age, and city in variables and print a sentence using all three.
Store a price and a quantity, then compute and print the total.
Read a number as text, convert it, and print double its value.
Swap the values of two variables and print them before and after.
Store a boolean for is raining and print a different message for true and false.

blocks.text: Once variables feel natural, you are ready to make your program act on them with operators and decisions. That is where things start to feel truly powerful.
